title: Telesat in advanced talks with Germany for interim satellite capabilities
html:
Telesat Corp. TSAT-T is in advanced discussions with the German armed forces to provide interim satellite capabilities while that country establishes its own low-earth-orbit capabilities, as governments aim to develop sovereign domestic space networks on concerns about control and security.

The Ottawa-based satellite operator and the German Bundeswehr are close to a deal that would grant its army interim access to Telesat’s low earth orbit constellation (LEO), Lightspeed, as Germany develops its own space network, according to a source with knowledge of the matter.

The company is also in early conversations with some other companies for similar services, according to the source. The Globe is not naming the source as they were not authorized to speak on the matter.

Global governments are currently seeking to build up their domestic satellite capabilities, amid a surge in defence spending and a desire to reduce reliance on foreign companies, and in particular, Elon Musk’s LEO constellation, Starlink. But the shortage of rocket launches to bring satellites into orbit means that for many, a home-grown network is still years away.

In a statement, Telesat said it does not comment on potential commercial discussions or strategic opportunities, but noted that its Lightspeed constellation is purpose-built with defence and government users in mind.

“We believe that it’s as close to a sovereign military SATCOM solution as you can get without building and launching your own constellation,” the company said in a statement.

Telesat has jumped on the opportunity to provide military services. Earlier this year, shares in the company soared after chief executive officer Dan Goldberg said the company is “increasingly bullish on the government and defence opportunity.”

The Bundeswehr declined to comment on specific contracts, but confirmed it plans to temporarily lease satellite communications services on the “open international market” while it develops its own constellation, which it says will be able to connect soldiers, drones, and aircraft in real time.

The planned constellation project, known as “SatComBw Stage 4,” will provide the armed forces with low latency, high data rates and high resilience “through the distributed architecture of a larger constellation.”

Telesat expects its network to be operational in 2028. Germany is targeting initial operational capability is targeted for 2031, with full operational capability expected by 2033.

Space is becoming an increasingly important miliary domain, and the reliance on this technology is driving concerns about third-party control and potential denial of service.

Experts have pointed to a recent example to demonstrate the risk: In mid-October, Ukrainian officials said SpaceX had ​abruptly capped the speed of Starlink and Starshield – the military version of Starlink – cutting off drones and other ‌equipment ⁠moving faster than about 160 km/h amid tensions with the Trump administration over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries.

In a post on X, Musk later acknowledged that his company SpaceX throttled the Starlink satellite internet service, saying that the Ukrainian military “violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people.”

But in November, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky once again said the military version of Starlink satellite internet that Kyiv relies upon to fight back against Russia was being throttled.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has said Canada, too, should diversify away from dependence on Mr. Musk’s company. Last year, Ontario cancelled a $100-million contract with Starlink to provide rural internet service on trade concerns. In August, Ottawa committed $2.3-billion to Telesat to develop next-generation military satellite communications.

However, Canada is still largely reliant on the company. Telesat’s Lightspeed satellites are scheduled to be launched into orbit aboard SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rockets starting in mid-2027.

Ottawa is supporting a push to develop domestic launch capabilities, with companies like Canada Rocket Co., NordSpace and Maritime Launch Services developing the technology and physical sites from which Canadian companies could one day send satellites to space, but those capabilities are still several years away.

Meanwhile, Telesat is facing another challenge: approximately US$1.71-billion in debt coming due Dec. 6, with another US$438-million of debt maturing in 2027.

In mid-November, the company came to a standstill agreement with debtholders to delay any enforcement actions on the Dec. 6 debt until Jan. 18, extending its runway by about a month and a half as it seeks to come to an agreement with lenders.
summary: Deal would give army access to low earth orbit constellation as Germany develops own network, source says
